title: World capitals
subtitle: All 195 countries
about: The 193 UN member states plus the two observer states, Vatican City and Palestine. Cards are grouped by UN region so neighbours are learned together.

cards.note: Named after the Parisii, an Iron Age Gallic tribe; the Romans called their town on the Seine Lutetia.
A city-state: the country is a single municipality. The old town, Monaco-Ville, sits on the Rock, seized by the Grimaldis in 1297 disguised as monks.
The name most likely comes from Old Dutch Bruocsella, 'settlement in the marsh'. It also hosts many of the European Union's principal institutions.
Literally 'dam in the Amstel'. It is the constitutional capital, but government, parliament and the supreme court have sat in The Hague since 1588.
Grew from Lucilinburhuc, 'small castle', acquired by Count Siegfried in 963; its mighty fortress earned it the nickname 'Gibraltar of the North'.
Split by the Berlin Wall from 1961 while Bonn served West Germany; after reunification in 1990, parliament voted to return to Berlin.
Officially the 'federal city', not the capital. Legend says founder Berthold V of Zähringen named it after the first animal he hunted: a bear.
A small town on the Rhine overlooked by Vaduz Castle, home of the reigning prince; neighbouring Schaan is actually larger.
Began as the Roman camp Vindobona on the Danube, and later served for centuries as the seat of the Habsburg emperors.
Founded by the Romans as Londinium on the Thames; its ancient core, the City of London, still keeps its medieval boundaries.
From Irish Dubh Linn, 'black pool', a dark tidal pool where the River Poddle met the Liffey, behind today's Dublin Castle.
Old Norse for 'smoky bay', said to be named for steam rising from hot springs; it is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state.
Its Danish name, København, means 'merchants' harbour'. Bishop Absalon built a fortress on Slotsholmen in 1167, where Christiansborg Palace now stands.
Rebuilt after a fire in 1624 and named Christiania after King Christian IV; the city took back the old name Oslo in 1925.
Spread across fourteen islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea; Gamla Stan, the old town, keeps its medieval street plan.
Founded by Gustav I of Sweden in 1550 to rival Tallinn; Russia's Alexander I made it the capital in 1812, replacing Turku.
Long known as Reval, the name is usually traced to Taani-linna, 'Danish castle'. Its medieval Hanseatic old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Founded in 1201 by the crusading Bishop Albert and later a Hanseatic city; its historic centre is famed for Art Nouveau architecture.
Legend says Grand Duke Gediminas dreamed of an iron wolf howling on a hill, a sign to build his capital there.
Largely destroyed by the earthquake of 1 November 1755 and rebuilt; the old Alfama district, whose name comes from Arabic, survived.
Began as a fortress built by the Umayyad emir Muhammad I; Philip II settled his royal court there permanently in 1561.
Set high in the eastern Pyrenees between France and Spain at 1,023 metres; it is the highest capital city in Europe.
The 'Eternal City', founded according to legend in 753 BC; it surrounds Vatican City, a whole country inside a city.
A city-state ruled by the pope, entirely enclosed by Rome; it was created by the Lateran Treaty with Italy in 1929.
Officially the City of San Marino, perched on the slopes of Monte Titano; tradition says Saint Marinus founded it in 301.
Built by the Knights Hospitaller after the Great Siege of 1565 and named after their victorious Grand Master, Jean de Valette.
Its emblem is the Ljubljana Dragon, which sits atop the castle tower on the city's coat of arms and guards the Dragon Bridge.
Grew from two rival hilltop towns: Kaptol, home of the clergy and cathedral, and Gradec, home of merchants; they were united in 1851.
Named from the Turkish saray, 'palace'. Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated there in 1914, and it hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.
Its name means 'White City'. It stands on the ridge where the Sava flows into the Danube.
The name means 'under the hill', after the small hill Gorica. It was called Titograd from 1946 until 1992.
Founded in 1614 by the Ottoman nobleman Sulejman Pasha around a mosque and bazaar; it was named Albania's capital in 1920.
An earthquake in 1963 destroyed about 80 percent of the city, which was then rebuilt with help from around the world.
Myth says Athena won the city by giving it the first olive tree, beating Poseidon; scholars think the goddess was named after the city.
Known in antiquity as Serdica; its modern name comes from the Saint Sofia Church, from the Greek sophia, 'wisdom'.
Tradition credits its founding to a man named Bucur, variously a prince, shepherd or fisherman; the Romanian word bucurie means 'joy'.
The name may come from archaic Romanian chișla nouă, 'new spring', because the town grew up around a small spring.
Straddles the Dnieper; the city's name is traditionally said to come from Kyi, one of its four legendary founders.
Created in 1873 by uniting Buda and Óbuda on the west bank of the Danube with Pest on the east bank.
Formerly Pressburg, coronation city of Hungarian kings; it is the only national capital that borders two other sovereign states, Austria and Hungary.
Nicknamed the 'City of a Hundred Spires' after a count by the mathematician Bernard Bolzano; Charles Bridge crosses the Vltava below Prague Castle.
Sigismund III moved the royal court there from Kraków in 1596. About 85 percent of the city was destroyed in World War II, then rebuilt.
First mentioned in 1067 in connection with the Battle on the River Nemiga; it stands on the Svislach river.
First documented in 1147. Peter the Great moved the capital to Saint Petersburg in 1712; it returned to Moscow in 1918.
Chosen by Queen Victoria in 1857 as a compromise between rival cities; the name comes from the Ottawa River, from Algonquin adawe, 'to trade'.
Named after George Washington; the district was created on the Potomac by the Residence Act of 1790, and Congress moved there from Philadelphia in 1800.
Built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, the Mexica city founded around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco; it is still slowly sinking.
Purpose-built inland after Hurricane Hattie devastated Belize City in 1961; the name joins the Belize and Mopan rivers.
Founded after the 1773 Santa Marta earthquakes ruined the old capital, now called Antigua Guatemala; its formal name means 'New Guatemala'.
'Holy Saviour', named by Spanish conquistadors in 1525; it sits in a valley ringed by volcanoes and is prone to earthquakes.
Became the capital in 1880, replacing Comayagua; the constitution makes it and its twin city Comayagüela a single Central District.
Lies on the shore of Lake Managua; the name may come from Nahuatl for 'adjacent to the water'. Earthquakes in 1931 and 1972 devastated it.
Named after Saint Joseph, the parish patron; it became the capital in 1823, taking over from the colonial capital Cartago.
Founded in 1519 by Pedro Arias Dávila; after the privateer Henry Morgan burned it in 1671, it was rebuilt on a new site.
Founded in 1538 by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada on the Andean plateau of the Muisca; the name comes from the Muisca settlement Bacatá.
The capital city closest to the Equator; in 1978 its historic centre and Kraków's became UNESCO's first World Heritage cultural sites.
Founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 as the City of Kings, after the Epiphany; the name Lima comes from Limaq, a famous Quechua oracle.
Founded by the conquistador Pedro de Valdivia in 1541 on the Mapocho River, with the snowy Andes rising behind it.
Sucre is the constitutional capital and seat of the judiciary, named after independence leader Antonio José de Sucre; La Paz is the seat of government.
A fort founded on 15 August 1537, the feast of the Assumption; expeditions from it founded other cities, earning the nickname 'Mother of Cities'.
'Fair winds': Pedro de Mendoza named it Holy Mary of the Fair Winds, after a Virgin that Spanish sailors invoked for safe voyages.
A Spanish fortified town of the 1720s on the Río de la Plata; it hosted every match of the first World Cup in 1930.
Planned city inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro; Lúcio Costa laid it out like an aeroplane, with buildings by Oscar Niemeyer.
Named after the Paramaribo people of the Suriname River's mouth; its wooden Dutch colonial inner city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Renamed in 1812 in honour of King George III; it lies below high tide level, protected by a seawall and drained by Dutch-style canals.
Founded in 1567 by Diego de Losada as Santiago de León de Caracas; the steep Ávila range separates its valley from the Caribbean.
Founded by the Spanish as Puerto de España on the Gulf of Paria; it replaced inland San José de Oruña as capital in 1757.
Wrapped around a horseshoe-shaped harbour, with the hillside of an old volcanic crater rising behind the town.
Its botanical garden, begun in 1765, is one of the oldest in the Western Hemisphere; Captain Bligh of the Bounty brought breadfruit there.
English settlers found a bridge built by Indigenous people and called the area Indian Bridge; Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison is a UNESCO site.
Named after the Marquis de Castries, a French naval minister; it has been rebuilt many times after great fires, most notably in 1948.
French settlers named it after the river reeds, roseaux, that grew thickly along the banks of the Roseau River.
Laid out on St. John's Harbour after a French invasion in 1666; it was the seat of government of the British Leeward Islands until 1959.
French for 'low land'; one of the oldest towns in the Eastern Caribbean, its central roundabout, the Circus, was modelled on Piccadilly Circus.
Founded in the 1490s by Bartholomew Columbus, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.
'Prince's Port': one theory says it was named after Le Prince, a French ship that arrived in 1706. A massive earthquake struck it in 2010.
Founded in 1692 to house survivors of the earthquake that destroyed the pirate haven of Port Royal across the harbour.
Founded by the Spanish in 1519, its strategic harbour made it Cuba's capital by 1552; Old Havana is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Named in honour of William III of England, Prince of Orange-Nassau; on New Providence island, it was once a notorious pirate stronghold.
A planned capital created as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne, designed by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin.
Named after the Duke of Wellington, victor of Waterloo; capital since 1865, it is the southernmost capital of a sovereign state.
Captain John Moresby charted the harbour in 1873 and named it after his father, Admiral Fairfax Moresby; Motu and Koitabu people lived there long before.
On Guadalcanal, near Henderson Field, fought over in 1942; the infrastructure the Americans built persuaded Britain to move the capital there in 1952.
On the island of Efate; the name Vila comes from Efil, the local South Efate name for the area, and it was a wartime airbase.
Became the capital in 1877, replacing Levuka, which was squeezed between a steep mountain and the sea with no room to grow.
A purpose-built seat of government on Babeldaob that replaced Koror in 2006; the name means 'place of fermented angelfish', once offered to the gods.
A purpose-built capital on the volcanic island of Pohnpei, declared in 1989; it replaced the nearby coastal town of Kolonia.
Both a coral atoll of over 60 islands and the capital; its main centre is Delap-Uliga-Djarrit, three islets joined together.
Nauru has no official capital and no cities; government offices and parliament sit in Yaren District, once called Makwa after an underground lake.
A string of islets on Tarawa atoll joined by causeways; Betio, at its western end, saw the bloody Battle of Tarawa in 1943.
An atoll of many islets around a lagoon; Americans built its airfield during World War II, and the main islet Fongafale holds the government centre.
Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years here and is buried on Mount Vaea; in 1889 a typhoon wrecked rival warships in its harbour.
On the north coast of Tongatapu, home to the Royal Palace and parliament; the name is commonly translated as 'abode of love'.
Its name comes from ribat, a fortified base; the Almohads founded it in the 12th century as a naval stronghold.
From Arabic al-Jazāʾir, 'the islands', after islets off its harbour; the whole country, Algeria, was later named after the city.
Its old medina is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the site of ancient Carthage now lies among its seaside suburbs.
From Greek Tripolis, 'three cities': Oea, Sabratha and Leptis Magna. Only Oea survived antiquity, growing into today's Tripoli.
From al-Qāhira, 'the Vanquisher', founded by the Fatimids in 969. Since 2024 the government has sat in the New Capital, east of Cairo.
Stands where the White Nile and Blue Nile meet; the name may come from Arabic khurṭūm, 'trunk', for the narrow strip between them.
Portuguese for 'beach'. On the south coast of Santiago island, it became the capital in 1770, superseding Cidade Velha.
A small fishing town until 1958, it was built as the capital for independence in 1960; its name may mean 'place of the winds'.
Sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of mainland Africa, and replaced Saint-Louis as capital of French West Africa in 1902.
Built on St Mary's Island, where the Gambia River meets the Atlantic, it was called Bathurst until 1973.
Founded in 1687 as a Portuguese trading post on the Geba River estuary; it replaced Bolama as the colonial capital in 1941.
Began on little Tombo Island, one of the Îles de Los, then spread along the Kaloum Peninsula reaching into the Atlantic.
Founded in 1792 by over a thousand formerly enslaved African Americans arriving from Nova Scotia; their first service was held under a great Cotton Tree.
Named after US President James Monroe; with Washington, D.C., it is one of only two capitals named after an American president.
President Houphouët-Boigny's birthplace, made capital in 1983; Abidjan, the former capital, remains the official economic capital and largest city.
Its name means 'crocodile river' in Bambara; the city lies on the Niger River near rapids dividing the upper and middle Niger.
Long the seat of the Mossi rulers, the Moro Naba; today it hosts FESPACO, Africa's largest film and television festival.
From the Akan word nkran, 'ants', after the anthills around it; it replaced Cape Coast as capital of the Gold Coast in 1877.
From Ewe Alomé, 'in the alo trees'. It sits on the Gulf of Guinea against the Ghana border, and became German Togoland's capital in 1897.
Portuguese for 'new port'. It is the official capital, where the legislature sits, while nearby Cotonou is the seat of government.
On the Niger River; it became capital of the French colony in 1926, replacing Zinder, which lay too close to the Nigerian border.
A planned city chosen for its central, neutral location; it replaced Lagos as capital in 1991 and sits beside the Aso Rock monolith.
Founded by the French as Fort-Lamy, after officer Amédée-François Lamy; renamed in the 1970s, from Arabic meaning 'place of rest'.
Founded in 1889 as a French outpost on the Ubangi River, whose name refers to the rapids there that ended navigation north from Brazzaville.
Founded by German explorers in 1887 as a trading post for rubber and ivory; it is the capital, though the port of Douala is larger.
Spanish for 'City of Peace': a planned city on the mainland, formerly Oyala; a January 2026 decree moved the capital here from Malabo on Bioko.
Portuguese for 'Saint Thomas'. Its Fort São Sebastião, built in 1566, now houses the national museum.
French for 'free town': founded in 1849 for people freed from the captured slave ship L'Elizia, on the Gabon Estuary just north of the equator.
Named after explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza; it faces Kinshasa across the Congo River and served as Free France's capital early in World War II.
Named Léopoldville by Stanley after Belgium's Leopold II; renamed in 1966, after the village of Nshasa, under Mobutu's Zairianisation campaign.
Founded in 1576 by the Portuguese explorer Paulo Dias de Novais as São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda, among Africa's oldest colonial cities.
Nicknamed Piccola Roma, 'Little Rome', under Italian rule; its Italian modernist architecture became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.
Founded by the French in 1888 on the Gulf of Tadjoura; it grew as the sea terminus of the railway to Addis Ababa.
Amharic for 'new flower'. Founded by Menelik II in 1886 around hot mineral springs, it is the highest capital in Africa.
Known locally as Xamar; a wealthy medieval sultanate based here controlled the Indian Ocean gold trade for centuries.
On the White Nile; it became capital at independence in 2011, and a planned move to Ramciel has been announced but not yet carried out.
From 'hill of the impala': the hill was a royal hunting ground of the Kabaka of Buganda before the British built a fort on it.
From the Maasai Enkare Nyirobi, 'place of cool waters'; unusually, a national park lies within the city's boundaries.
Named after Mount Kigali, from a word meaning 'broad'; founded in 1907 as a German outpost, it became capital at independence in 1962.
The former royal capital became the political capital again in 2019; Bujumbura, on Lake Tanganyika, remains the economic capital.
Its name means 'it has sunk' in Gogo. Chosen in 1974 for its central location, it officially replaced Dar es Salaam in 1996.
Named after the Lilongwe River; it replaced Zomba as capital in 1975, a move meant to spur growth in central and northern Malawi.
Began as a railway water stop named after the Lenje chief Lusaaka; it became capital of Northern Rhodesia in 1935, replacing Livingstone.
Founded in 1890 as Fort Salisbury, after the British prime minister Lord Salisbury; renamed Harare in 1982, two years after independence.
Called Lourenço Marques until 1976, after the Portuguese navigator who explored the bay in 1544.
Its name means 'at the river' in Shingazidja; it lies on Ngazidja, the largest of the three main islands.
Means 'City of the Thousand', honouring the thousand soldiers King Andrianjaka used to capture and guard its hilltop site.
Founded by French settlers as L'Établissement on Mahé; the British renamed it in 1841 after Queen Victoria.
Named in honour of King Louis XV; under French rule from 1736 it became a key stop for ships sailing round the Cape.
Usually read as Afrikaans for 'windy corner', though it may instead honour the Winterhoek Mountains in South Africa.
Named after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa and built from 1964; the colonial capital, Mafeking, actually lay outside the territory.
Pretoria is the executive capital, Cape Town the legislative and Bloemfontein the judicial: a compromise struck at Union in 1910.
Sesotho for 'red sandstones'; founded as a British police camp in 1869 on the Caledon River, right on the South African border.
Mbabane, named after Chief Mbabane Kunene, is the executive capital; nearby Lobamba is the royal and legislative capital, home of the Reed Dance.
Ancient Ankyra, Greek for 'anchor'. As Angora it lent its name to Angora goats, rabbits and cats; it became capital in 1923.
Divided by the Green Line since 1974, it is Lefkosia in Greek and Lefkoşa in Turkish; its Venetian walls form a star with eleven bastions.
From tbili, 'warm', after its sulphur springs; legend says King Vakhtang founded it after his falcon and its pheasant prey fell into a hot spring.
Traces its origin to the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BC; Mount Ararat dominates its skyline.
On the Caspian shore of the Absheron Peninsula, 28 metres below sea level, making it the lowest-lying national capital in the world.
One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities; it was capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, which built its Great Mosque in the 700s.
From the Phoenician word for 'wells'. Roman Berytus had a renowned law school where the jurists Papinian and Ulpian taught.
Israel's proclaimed capital and seat of government, but its status is internationally disputed; most countries keep their embassies in Tel Aviv.
Palestine claims East Jerusalem as its capital; Ramallah, whose name means 'height of God', is the de facto administrative seat.
Once Rabbath Ammon, capital of the Ammonites; Ptolemy II renamed it Philadelphia. It was originally built on seven hills.
Founded in 762 by Caliph al-Mansur as a Round City on the Tigris, officially named Madinat al-Salam, the 'City of Peace'.
Kuwait is a diminutive of Arabic kut, a fortress built near water; the city lies on Kuwait Bay, marked by the Kuwait Towers.
Means 'gardens', recalling earlier oasis towns. Ibn Saud's capture of its Masmak fortress in 1902 is a celebrated moment in Saudi history.
Possibly from Arabic for 'place of rest' or 'place of dreams'; the town is first named in a manuscript dating from 1345.
From Arabic dohat, 'roundness', for the rounded bays of its coast; it was declared the capital at independence in 1971.
Arabic for 'father of the gazelle'. It stands on a T-shaped island; its oldest building, the Qasr al-Hosn fort, dates from 1761.
Backed by the Hajar Mountains; its Al Jalali and Al Mirani forts are the most prominent buildings left by the Portuguese.
Possibly 'well-fortified' in Sabaic. Held by the Houthis since 2014, so in 2015 the recognised government declared Aden a temporary capital.
Simply means 'capital' in Kazakh; it replaced Almaty in 1997 and was briefly called Nur-Sultan from 2019 to 2022.
Called Frunze from 1926 to 1991, after the Bolshevik Mikhail Frunze; Bishkek supposedly names a paddle used to churn kumis, fermented milk.
Means 'Monday' in Tajik Persian, after its weekly Monday bazaar; it was named Stalinabad from 1929 to 1961.
Means 'stone city', from Turkic tash and Persian kent; it was rebuilt as a model Soviet city after the 1966 earthquake.
Often glossed as 'city of love'. Rebuilt after the 1948 earthquake, it holds a Guinness record for its density of white marble buildings.
Its name is often read as 'bottom of the mountain', fitting its site below the Alborz range; it became capital in 1786 under the Qajars.
Lies in a narrow Hindu Kush valley on the Kabul River, about 1,790 metres up; the Mughal emperor Babur chose to be buried here.
Means 'City of Islam'. A planned city of the 1960s at the foot of the Margalla Hills, it replaced Karachi as the capital.
Announced at the 1911 Delhi Durbar to replace Calcutta as capital, it was planned by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker and inaugurated in 1931.
Named after the Kasthamandap, a Sanskrit 'wooden pavilion' said to use no iron nails; its medieval name was Kantipur.
Took over from the ancient capital Punakha in the 1950s; its Tashichho Dzong, 'fortress of the glorious religion', houses the king's throne room.
Named Jahangirnagar, after the Mughal emperor, when it became the capital of Mughal Bengal in 1610; nicknamed the City of Mosques.
'Resplendent city of growing victory', capital of the medieval Kotte kingdom, has housed Parliament since 1982; neighbouring Colombo is the commercial capital.
An island city of under two square kilometres on the edge of North Malé Atoll, linked to Hulhulé by the Sinamalé Bridge since 2018.
Means 'northern capital'; China's political centre for most of the past eight centuries, it was renamed Beiping while Nanjing was capital.
Means 'Red Hero', adopted in 1924. It began in 1639 as a mobile yurt monastery that moved dozens of times before settling in 1778.
Means 'flat land'. On the Taedong River, it was poetically called Ryugyong, the 'Capital of Willows'.
Seoul is simply a native Korean word for 'capital'; founded as Hanyang for the Joseon dynasty in 1394, it straddles the Han River.
Means 'eastern capital'. Formerly Edo, 'estuary', it was renamed in 1868 when Emperor Meiji moved the capital from Kyoto.
Burmese for 'abode of the king'; it replaced Yangon as capital in 2005, and its 20-lane boulevard is largely empty.
Thais call it Krung Thep, 'City of Angels'; its full ceremonial name holds the Guinness record as the world's longest place name.
Means 'walled city of sandalwood'. On the Mekong close to the Thai border, it became Lan Xang's capital under King Setthathirath in 1563.
Means 'Penh's hill', after Lady Penh, who built a hilltop shrine, now Wat Phnom; it sits where the Tonlé Sap meets the Mekong.
Means 'inside the rivers', named in 1831; founded in 1010 as Thăng Long, 'ascending dragon', after a dragon seen rising over the Red River.
Malay for 'muddy confluence', where the Gombak and Klang rivers meet; the executive and judiciary have moved to Putrajaya.
A city-state; its name comes from Sanskrit Siṃhapura, 'lion city', and Stamford Raffles set up a British trading post there in 1819.
Formerly Brunei Town, renamed in 1970 after Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III, the 'Seri Begawan'; Kampong Ayer is its vast stilt village.
Batavia under the Dutch. Sinking land and congestion prompted a planned move of the capital to Nusantara on Borneo, now targeted for 2028.
On Timor's north coast, it became the Portuguese colonial capital in 1769, replacing Lifau; a 27-metre Cristo Rei statue stands on a nearby headland.
From Maynilà, 'where nilad grows', a mangrove shrub; the Spanish built its walled city, Intramuros, from 1571.
